content: Scarlet fever is a disease caused by exotoxins, most commonly associated with a sore throat, though it can occasionally occur with impetigo or other streptococcal infections. The condition is characterized by a sore throat, fever, a strawberry appearance of the tongue, and a fine, sandpaper-like rash that typically begins on the upper body and may spread to cover nearly the entire body. While scarlet fever is distinct from rheumatic fever, it has the potential to progress into rheumatic fever, which is an autoimmune condition that can develop following an infection with Group A Streptococcus. This infectious disease primarily affects children between the ages of 4 and 8 years. The symptoms include a sore throat, fever, and a distinctive red rash. Scarlet fever is transmitted primarily through inhalation of respiratory droplets. There is currently no vaccine available for this disease, but it is effectively managed with antibiotic therapy. Before the advent of antibiotics, scarlet fever was a significant cause of mortality and could lead to severe complications such as glomerulonephritis and endocarditis, which often resulted in heart valve damage. These complications were prolonged and frequently fatal in the pre-antibiotic era. The causative agent of scarlet fever is the erythrogenic toxin produced by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) when the bacterium is infected by a specific bacteriophage. The term scarlatina is sometimes used interchangeably with scarlet fever, though it is more commonly employed to describe a milder form of the disease that has been observed since the early 20th century. Scarlet fever predominantly affects children, much like other common childhood illnesses such as colds or the flu. It is most frequently seen in children aged 3 to 15 years, with no significant difference in incidence between males and females. By the age of 10, most children have developed protective antibodies, making the occurrence of scarlet fever in older children or adults rare. The diagnosis of scarlet fever is primarily clinical. Laboratory findings may include marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia, conserved or elevated eosinophil counts, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, and an increased antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer. Blood cultures are rarely positive, but throat cultures typically confirm the presence of streptococci. The treatment of scarlet fever is similar to that of streptococcal pharyngitis. Antibiotics, particularly penicillin, are the standard therapy. For patients with penicillin allergies, alternative antibiotics such as clindamycin or erythromycin are effective. While antibiotic treatment is essential for managing the infection, it has not been definitively proven to reduce the risk of developing rheumatic fever.
